title: The Ear of Corn

full_text:
In ancient times, when the earth was young and humanity walked in harmony with nature, stalks of wheat grew five hundred times more abundantly than they do today. Every stalk bore grains along its entire length, from the root all the way to the tip, providing food in boundless abundance without heavy toil.

One afternoon, a foolish and arrogant woman walked through the village street holding her little child. The child slipped and fell into a muddy puddle, soiling its clothes. Without a thought of gratitude or reverence, the wasteful woman snatched a handful of golden wheat ears from the roadside stalk and used them to wipe the mud from her child's boots.

At that very moment, a voice of divine indignation echoed through the heavens: "Because humanity scorns the sacred bread that nourishes life, no stalk shall ever bear grain again!"

The peasants fell upon their knees in the dust, weeping and begging for mercy, pleading that even if mortals were unworthy, the innocent birds of the air and the beasts of the field must not starve.

Moved by their contrite repentance, the heavens showed mercy: the top of the stalk alone was permitted to bear an ear of grain, while the rest remained bare straw, reminding all generations to treat daily bread with humble gratitude and reverence.
moral: Bread is a sacred gift to be revered; wasteful arrogance brings scarcity and hard toil.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Ear of Corn"?
options: Presence of mind and quiet wisdom triumph over brute strength.
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof

By running away from every problem

quiz.question: What memorable conclusion does this story teach young readers?
